title: Angular Acceleration
lead: Uniform circular motion holds the angular velocity constant, but a skater who pulls in her arms, a merry-go-round a child starts from rest and a hard disk that slows to a halt all change their rate of spin. This section defines angular acceleration as the rate of change of angular velocity, works it through for a bicycle wheel spun up and then braked, separates the tangential acceleration that changes the speed of a point on a circle from the centripetal acceleration that changes its direction, and ties the tangential acceleration to the angular acceleration by the radius, exactly as the linear velocity was tied to the angular velocity.
objectives: Calculate angular acceleration of an object.
Observe the link between linear and angular acceleration.
summary_html:
• Uniform circular motion is the motion with a constant angular velocity $\kw = \frac{\Delta\theta}{\kdt}$.
  • In non-uniform circular motion, the velocity changes with time and the rate of change of angular velocity (i.e. angular acceleration) is $\kalpha = \frac{\kdw}{\kdt}$.
  • Linear or tangential acceleration refers to changes in the magnitude of velocity but not its direction, given as $\kat = \frac{\kdv}{\kdt}$.
  • For circular motion, note that $\kv = \kr\kw$, so that $$\kat = \frac{\Delta(\kr\kw)}{\kdt}.$$
  • The radius $\kr$ is constant for circular motion, and so $\Delta(\kr\kw) = \kr\kdw$. Thus, $$\kat = \kr\frac{\kdw}{\kdt}.$$
  • By definition, $\kdw/\kdt = \kalpha$. Thus, $$\kat = \kr\kalpha$$ or $$\kalpha = \frac{\kat}{\kr}.$$

figures.original_caption: This figure shows uniform circular motion and some of its defined quantities.

In circular motion, linear acceleration a, occurs as the magnitude of the velocity changes: a is tangent to the motion. In the context of circular motion, linear acceleration is also called tangential acceleration a_t. Centripetal acceleration a_c occurs as the direction of velocity changes; it is perpendicular to the circular motion. Centripetal and tangential acceleration are thus perpendicular to each other.
The linear acceleration of a motorcycle is accompanied by an angular acceleration of its wheels.

exercises.prompt: Angular acceleration is a vector, having both magnitude and direction. How do we denote its magnitude and direction? Illustrate with an example.

answer.solution: The magnitude of angular acceleration is $\kalpha$ and its most common units are $\text{rad/s}^2$. The direction of angular acceleration along a fixed axis is denoted by a + or a – sign, just as the direction of linear acceleration in one dimension is denoted by a + or a – sign. For example, consider a gymnast doing a forward flip. Her angular momentum would be parallel to the mat and to her left. The magnitude of her angular acceleration would be proportional to her angular velocity (spin rate) and her moment of inertia about her spin axis.

exercises.prompt: Analogies exist between rotational and translational physical quantities. Identify the rotational term analogous to each of the following: acceleration, force, mass, work, translational kinetic energy, linear momentum, impulse.

answer.solution: Begin with the three pairs Table 10.1 already gives, in which the angle stands for the position, the angular velocity for the velocity and the angular acceleration for the acceleration, so the rotational term analogous to acceleration is the angular acceleration $\kalpha$. The rest of the chapter builds the remaining pairs in the same way, each rotational quantity playing the part in a turning motion that its translational partner plays in a straight-line one. The analog of force is torque, the turning effectiveness of a force, which Statics and Torque introduced. The analog of mass is the moment of inertia, the resistance of a body to having its rotation changed, which depends on how the mass is spread about the axis and not only on how much there is. Work becomes the torque times the angle turned through, just as work in a straight line is the force times the distance moved. Translational kinetic energy, one half the mass times the square of the speed, becomes rotational kinetic energy, one half the moment of inertia times the square of the angular velocity. Linear momentum, mass times velocity, becomes angular momentum, moment of inertia times angular velocity. Impulse, the force times the time it acts, becomes the torque times the time it acts, which changes the angular momentum as an impulse changes the linear momentum.

exercises.prompt: Explain why centripetal acceleration changes the direction of velocity in circular motion but not its magnitude.

answer.solution: An acceleration changes the velocity in the direction the acceleration points. Centripetal acceleration always points toward the center of the circle, and the velocity of an object in circular motion is always tangent to the circle, so at every instant the centripetal acceleration is perpendicular to the velocity. A change in velocity that is perpendicular to the velocity itself can only turn the velocity vector; it adds nothing along the direction of motion and takes nothing away from it, so the speed is unchanged. Only a component of acceleration along the velocity, which is what the tangential acceleration is, could make the object move faster or more slowly. That is why an object in uniform circular motion, which has centripetal acceleration and nothing else, keeps a constant speed while its direction of travel turns continuously.

exercises.prompt: In circular motion, a tangential acceleration can change the magnitude of the velocity but not its direction. Explain your answer.

answer.solution: The tangential acceleration is tangent to the circle at the point of interest, which is exactly the direction the velocity has there. An acceleration along the line of the velocity lengthens or shortens the velocity vector without swinging it to one side, so it changes the speed and leaves the direction of travel as it was. Turning the velocity is the work of the centripetal acceleration, which is perpendicular to it. Because the two accelerations are perpendicular they are independent of one another, and the tangential acceleration on its own can only speed the object up along the circle or slow it down, as the brakes on the bicycle wheel of Example 10.1 slow every point on the rim without changing the circle it moves on.

exercises.prompt: Suppose a piece of food is on the edge of a rotating microwave oven plate. Does it experience nonzero tangential acceleration, centripetal acceleration, or both when: (a) The plate starts to spin? (b) The plate rotates at constant angular velocity? (c) The plate slows to a halt?

answer.solution: Ask two questions at each stage: is the speed of the food changing, and is the food moving in a circle at all? A changing speed means a tangential acceleration, since $\kat = \kr\kalpha$ is nonzero whenever the angular velocity is changing, and any motion in a circle means a centripetal acceleration, since $\kac = \kr\kw^2$ is nonzero whenever the angular velocity is. (a) As the plate starts to spin its angular velocity is increasing, so the food has a tangential acceleration, and as soon as it is moving in its circle it has a centripetal acceleration as well, so it experiences both. (b) At constant angular velocity the speed is constant and the tangential acceleration is zero, but the food is still moving in a circle, so it has a centripetal acceleration and nothing else. (c) As the plate slows the angular velocity is decreasing, so there is a tangential acceleration directed against the motion, and while the food is still turning there is a centripetal acceleration too, so again it experiences both; at the instant the plate halts both fall to zero.

exercises.prompt: At its peak, a tornado is 60.0 m in diameter and carries 500 km/h winds. What is its angular velocity in revolutions per second?

answer.hint: The wind at the edge is the linear velocity of a point at the radius, which is half the diameter. Convert the speed to meters per second, use $\kw = \kv/\kr$ to find the angular velocity in radians per second, and then remember that one revolution is $2\pi$ radians.
